topics.topic: What Magnets Can Do — Properties of Magnets

easy.question: Which of the following materials will be attracted by a magnet?
options: Steel safety pin
Wooden ruler
Plastic bottle cap
Rubber eraser
easy.explanation: Steel contains iron, which is a magnetic material. Wood, plastic, and rubber are all non-magnetic materials and are not attracted by a magnet.

easy.question: How many poles does every magnet have?
options: Two
One
Three
It depends on the shape of the magnet
easy.explanation: Every magnet — regardless of its shape or size — always has exactly two poles: a North Pole and a South Pole.

easy.question: What happens when the south pole of one magnet is brought near the south pole of another magnet?
options: They repel each other
They attract each other
Nothing happens
They stick together permanently
easy.explanation: Like poles (south-south or north-north) always repel each other. Only unlike poles (north-south) attract.

easy.question: The magnetic force of a magnet is strongest at its ______.
easy.explanation: The two poles of a magnet are where the magnetic force is at its maximum. The force is weakest at the middle of the magnet.

easy.question: Give two examples of magnetic materials and two examples of non-magnetic materials.
easy.answer: Magnetic materials: iron nail, steel spoon (also accept cobalt, nickel). Non-magnetic materials: glass marble, wooden stick (also accept plastic, rubber, copper, aluminium).
easy.explanation: Magnetic materials are attracted by magnets and include iron, steel, cobalt, and nickel. Non-magnetic materials such as glass, wood, plastic, rubber, copper, and aluminium are not affected by magnets.

medium.question: Riya holds a magnet near an aluminium spoon. What will she observe?
options: The spoon will not be attracted to the magnet
The spoon will stick strongly to the magnet
The spoon will be weakly attracted
The spoon will become a permanent magnet
medium.answer: The spoon will not be attracted to the magnet
medium.explanation: Aluminium is a non-magnetic material even though it is a metal. A magnet will have no attractive effect on it.

medium.question: A student claims that all metals are attracted by magnets. Is this statement correct? Explain with examples.
medium.answer: The statement is incorrect. Only certain metals — iron, steel, cobalt, and nickel — are attracted by magnets. Many metals such as copper, aluminium, gold, and silver are non-magnetic and are not attracted by a magnet.
medium.explanation: Being a metal does not automatically make a substance magnetic. Magnetism depends on the internal atomic structure of the material, not simply on whether it is a metal.

medium.question: When a north pole is brought near a south pole, they ______ each other, but when two north poles are brought together, they ______ each other.
medium.explanation: Unlike poles (north and south) attract, while like poles (north-north or south-south) repel. This is a fundamental property of magnets.

hard.question: Ankit has a box full of iron nails mixed with wooden matchsticks and plastic buttons. Describe a method he can use to quickly separate the iron nails from the other items. Explain why this method works.
hard.answer: Ankit can move a strong magnet slowly over the mixture. The iron nails will be attracted to the magnet and stick to it, while the wooden matchsticks and plastic buttons will remain in the box because they are non-magnetic materials. He can then pull the nails off the magnet and collect them separately. This works because iron is a magnetic material — it responds to the magnetic force — whereas wood and plastic are non-magnetic and are completely unaffected by the magnet.
hard.explanation: Magnets provide a quick and efficient way to separate magnetic materials (like iron) from non-magnetic materials (like wood and plastic) in a mixture.

hard.question: If you break a bar magnet exactly in half, how many poles will each piece have? Explain your reasoning.
hard.answer: Each piece will still have two poles — a North Pole and a South Pole. It is impossible to obtain a magnet with only one pole. No matter how many times you break a magnet, every fragment will always have both a north and a south pole.
hard.explanation: Magnetism arises from the alignment of tiny magnetic domains. Even the smallest fragment of a magnet contains domains with both north and south orientations at opposite ends.

topics.topic: Finding the Poles and Using a Compass

easy.question: What is the main purpose of a magnetic compass?
options: To find direction
To measure the weight of objects
To check the temperature
To measure the length of a room
easy.explanation: A compass contains a freely rotating magnetic needle that always points in the north-south direction, helping us determine which way is north, south, east, or west.

easy.question: When a bar magnet is hung freely by a thread, it settles in which direction?
options: North-South
East-West
It keeps spinning
It points in a different direction every time
easy.explanation: A freely suspended magnet always aligns itself along the north-south direction because the Earth acts as a giant magnet and attracts the poles of the hanging magnet.

easy.question: The Earth behaves like a giant ______.
easy.explanation: The Earth has a magnetic field generated by its molten iron-nickel core. This is why compass needles align along the north-south direction.

easy.question: Name the naturally occurring magnetic rock and the region in ancient Greece where it was first discovered.
easy.answer: The naturally occurring magnetic rock is called lodestone (or magnetite). It was discovered near a region called Magnesia in ancient Greece.
easy.explanation: The word 'magnet' itself is derived from Magnesia, the place where these naturally magnetic rocks were first found.

medium.question: Why does the north pole of a compass needle point toward the geographic North Pole of the Earth?
options: Because the geographic North Pole is near the Earth's magnetic south pole, and unlike poles attract
Because the geographic North Pole is near the Earth's magnetic north pole, and like poles attract
Because the compass needle is pushed by the Sun's rays
Because all needles naturally point north due to gravity
medium.answer: Because the geographic North Pole is near the Earth's magnetic south pole, and unlike poles attract
medium.explanation: The Earth's geographic North Pole lies close to its magnetic south pole. Since unlike poles attract, the north-seeking pole of the compass needle is pulled toward geographic north.

medium.question: Describe a simple method to find the North Pole and South Pole of an unmarked bar magnet.
medium.answer: Tie a thread around the centre of the bar magnet and let it hang freely so it can rotate without touching anything. Wait for it to stop moving. The end that points toward geographic north is the North Pole, and the opposite end is the South Pole.
medium.explanation: A freely suspended magnet aligns with the Earth's magnetic field. The end attracted toward geographic north is identified as the magnet's North Pole.

medium.question: The geographic North Pole of the Earth is actually close to the Earth's magnetic ______ pole.
medium.explanation: This is why the north pole of a compass needle is attracted toward the geographic north — because unlike poles attract each other.

hard.question: Meera placed a compass on a table and noticed the needle was pointing north. She then placed a strong bar magnet right next to the compass. The needle swung and pointed in a different direction. Explain why this happened.
hard.answer: The compass needle normally aligns with the Earth's magnetic field and points north. However, when Meera placed a strong bar magnet near the compass, the bar magnet's magnetic field overpowered the much weaker magnetic field of the Earth at that spot. The compass needle then aligned with the bar magnet's field instead of the Earth's field, causing it to point in a different direction. If Meera removes the bar magnet, the needle will return to pointing north.
hard.explanation: A compass needle responds to the strongest magnetic field in its surroundings. A nearby bar magnet produces a field that is much stronger than the Earth's field at close range, so the needle follows the bar magnet's field.

easy.question: Which of the following is a method of making a magnet?
options: Stroking an iron nail with a magnet in one direction
Dipping an iron nail in water
Heating an iron nail on a stove
Painting an iron nail with red colour
easy.answer: Stroking an iron nail with a magnet in one direction
easy.explanation: Repeated stroking in a single direction with one pole of a magnet aligns the magnetic domains inside the iron nail, turning it into a magnet.

easy.question: An electromagnet works only when ______.
options: Electric current flows through the coil
It is placed in sunlight
It is dipped in water
It is kept in a refrigerator
easy.answer: Electric current flows through the coil
easy.explanation: An electromagnet is a temporary magnet that functions only when electric current passes through the wire coil wrapped around the iron core.

easy.question: The process of making a piece of iron into a magnet is called ______.
easy.explanation: Magnetisation is the process by which a non-magnetic piece of iron or steel is turned into a magnet, either by stroking or by using electric current.

easy.question: What is the difference between a permanent magnet and an electromagnet?
easy.answer: A permanent magnet retains its magnetism for a long time without any external source of energy. An electromagnet works only when electric current flows through it — switching off the current causes it to lose its magnetism.
easy.explanation: Permanent magnets (like bar magnets) keep their magnetism on their own, while electromagnets depend on electricity and can be turned on and off.

easy.question: Which of the following can cause a magnet to lose its magnetism?
options: Dropping it repeatedly on a hard floor
Wrapping it in a cloth
Keeping it on a wooden shelf
Placing it next to another magnet with unlike poles touching
easy.answer: Dropping it repeatedly on a hard floor
easy.explanation: Dropping a magnet repeatedly disturbs the alignment of its internal magnetic domains, causing it to lose its magnetism. This is called demagnetisation.

medium.question: Describe the steps to make a magnet using the stroking method.
medium.answer: 1. Hold a bar magnet in one hand and place one of its poles at one end of an iron nail. 2. Slide the magnet along the nail in one direction only — from one end to the other. 3. Lift the magnet, bring it back to the starting point, and repeat the stroke. 4. Continue for 30 to 40 strokes. 5. Test the nail by bringing it near iron filings or small pins — if they stick, the nail has been magnetised.
medium.explanation: Single-direction stroking aligns the magnetic domains inside the iron nail in the same direction, turning the nail into a temporary magnet.

medium.question: Which of these is NOT a correct way to take care of a magnet?
options: Hammering the magnet to make it stronger
Storing bar magnets in pairs with keepers
Keeping magnets away from electronic devices
Avoiding dropping magnets on hard surfaces
medium.answer: Hammering the magnet to make it stronger
medium.explanation: Hammering a magnet does not make it stronger — it actually weakens the magnet by disrupting the alignment of its internal magnetic domains.

medium.question: Give any three uses of magnets in everyday life.
medium.answer: 1. Refrigerator door seal — a magnetic strip holds the door shut. 2. Speakers and earphones — magnets help convert electrical signals into sound. 3. Magnetic compass — a magnetic needle shows direction for travellers. (Also accept: MRI machines, electric motors, maglev trains, cranes at scrapyards.)
medium.explanation: Magnets are used in a wide variety of devices and applications in daily life, from household appliances to advanced technology.

hard.question: Explain how an electromagnet is made. Why are electromagnets preferred over permanent magnets in scrapyard cranes?
hard.answer: An electromagnet is made by winding a coil of insulated copper wire around an iron nail or rod and connecting the wire to a battery or power source. When current flows, the iron core becomes magnetised and can attract magnetic materials. When the current is switched off, the magnetism disappears. Scrapyard cranes use electromagnets instead of permanent magnets because the crane needs to pick up heavy iron and steel loads and then release them at a different location. With an electromagnet, the operator simply switches off the current to drop the load. A permanent magnet cannot be turned off, so it would be impossible to release the scrap at the desired location.
hard.explanation: The ability to switch an electromagnet on and off makes it far more practical for tasks like lifting and releasing heavy iron objects in scrapyards.

hard.question: Priya's grandmother says that keeping a magnet near a mobile phone can damage it. Is this correct? Explain the science behind this advice and list two other precautions for storing magnets safely.
hard.answer: Yes, Priya's grandmother is correct. Strong magnets can interfere with the electronic sensors inside a mobile phone (such as the compass sensor and the display) and can potentially damage components that store data magnetically. The magnetic field may also affect the phone's speaker and other parts. Two other precautions: (1) Do not drop or hammer a magnet, as physical shocks disturb the alignment of magnetic domains and weaken the magnet. (2) Do not heat a magnet, because high temperatures scramble the domains and cause the magnet to lose its magnetism.
hard.explanation: Magnets produce fields that can interfere with electronic components. Proper magnet care also involves protecting the magnet itself from physical shocks and heat.
